questions_asked: Do passengers finish the body scan before they reach the belt to collect their bags?
On a busy morning, which step causes most of the piling up?
Out of roughly 100 bags going through the X-ray, how many usually get flagged for a closer look?
How many minutes does a closer manual inspection usually take?
How many passengers, one after another, can one open lane screen per hour?
How many passengers reach the checkpoint in a minute during a busy morning?
Of all passengers using a checkpoint on a typical day, what share is in Pre-Check?
When the line grows long, do most travelers switch to an open lane?
Do people tend to bring more bags and bins into the screening lane?
How long does checking one traveler's ID and boarding pass usually take?
expert_answers:
No — not necessarily, and in the described process the two are decoupled.

The passenger's belongings go through the X-ray on the conveyor belt while the passenger separately goes through the millimeter wave scanner or metal detector. These are parallel streams, so a passenger can reach the post-X-ray belt to collect bags before, at roughly the same time as, or after finishing the body scan, depending on the relative service times of the two streams and any queueing at each.

In practice the body scan (plus possible pat-down in Zone D) is often the longer or more variable step, so many passengers arrive at the belt and wait for their bags, but the reverse also occurs. The process does not enforce a fixed ordering between body-scan completion and belt arrival.

On a busy morning, the bottleneck is almost always the **X-ray/bag-screening stream and the downstream Zone D secondary screening**, not the ID check or the body scanner itself.

Reasons: the X-ray conveyor is a single shared resource per lane with a long, variable service time (bins, laptops, liquids, flagged items), and any bag flagged for additional search pulls a security officer off the line, creating a compounding slowdown. Body scanning is comparatively fast and parallelizable across lanes. ID check is quick and rarely the constraint.

So the piling up concentrates at the **queue feeding the X-ray lanes (Zone B) and at the post-X-ray belt**, where passengers wait for their belongings — with secondary screening (Zone D) as the main source of variance. This is an empirical judgment based on typical checkpoint behavior, not a precise measured value.

Roughly 5–15 out of 100 bags, i.e. on the order of 10%, is the usual flag rate for X-ray secondary screening at a US checkpoint. This is an empirical judgment, not a precise measured value; the rate varies with the mix of passengers, the items carried, and how aggressively the operator is set to flag. Pre-Check bags tend to be flagged at a lower rate than regular-lane bags.

Typically on the order of **1–3 minutes** for a routine manual bag inspection, with a central estimate around **2 minutes**. Simple re-scans or a quick swab are faster (under a minute); a full unpack-and-search, explosives-trace swab, or a pat-down can run **3–5 minutes or more**. The distribution is right-skewed, so a small fraction of inspections take much longer and drive most of the variance. This is an empirical judgment, not a precise measured value.

Roughly **100–200 passengers per hour per open lane**, with a central estimate around **150/hour** for a regular lane under normal conditions. This is an empirical judgment, not a precise measured value.

The range reflects real-world variation: a well-staffed lane with few flagged bags and experienced passengers can approach 200/hour, while a lane slowed by heavy bin use, many laptops/liquids, frequent secondary screening, or Pre-Check-style mixed flow can drop toward 100/hour or below. Pre-Check lanes run higher (often 200–300/hour) because passengers divest less and are flagged less often.

Roughly **10–30 passengers per minute** arriving at a single checkpoint during a busy morning peak, with a central estimate around **15–20/minute**. This is an empirical judgment, not a precise measured value.

The range reflects real-world variation: a large hub checkpoint at peak can approach 30/minute, while a smaller or moderately busy checkpoint runs nearer 10/minute. Note this is the *arrival* rate; it should be compared against lane capacity (roughly 150/hour per lane, i.e. ~2.5/minute per lane) to see how many lanes must be open to keep the queue stable.

Roughly **40–50%**, with a central estimate around **45%** — the problem statement itself cites about 45% enrollment in Pre-Check. This is an empirical judgment for a typical US checkpoint; the actual share varies by airport and time of day, and is often lower at smaller airports and higher at large hubs with many frequent/business travelers.

No — most travelers do not switch lanes when the line grows long.

In a standard checkpoint, passengers commit to a lane once they enter the Zone B queue feeding a specific screening line; the physical layout (railings, single-file queue, belongings already on the belt) makes switching impractical or impossible. Travelers generally stay in their chosen lane and wait.

Switching mainly happens at the earlier stage — when a passenger is choosing which lane to join — and even then most people pick the nearest or shortest-looking queue and stay. The social norm against "cutting" (noted in the problem) further discourages mid-queue lane changes. So a long line mostly lengthens waiting rather than redistributing passengers across open lanes. This is an empirical judgment, not a measured value.

Yes — most passengers bring multiple items into the lane, not just one bag.

Typical travelers arrive with a carry-on plus a personal item (purse, backpack, laptop bag), and each of those plus the divested items (shoes, belt, jacket, electronics, liquids, laptop) goes into its own bin. So a single passenger commonly occupies **2–4 bins** on the belt, and a family or a heavy traveler can occupy considerably more.

This matters because bin count, not passenger count, is what loads the X-ray conveyor: more bins per passenger means longer belt occupancy and slower effective throughput per lane. Pre-Check passengers use fewer bins (no shoe/belt/jacket removal, laptop stays in bag), which is a large part of why their lanes run faster. This is an empirical judgment, not a measured value.

Typically on the order of **10–20 seconds** per traveler for a routine ID and boarding-pass check, with a central estimate around **15 seconds**. This is an empirical judgment, not a precise measured value.

The range reflects real-world variation: a quick glance-and-wave for a familiar or Pre-Check traveler can be under 10 seconds, while a slower check (document scrutiny, questions, a traveler fumbling for documents, or a flagged boarding pass) can run 30 seconds or more. It is one of the fastest steps in the checkpoint and rarely the bottleneck.
